newsitem.title: USA: Comcast brings cable modem to more areas.
newsitem.headline: Comcast brings cable modem to more areas.

text.p: Comcast Corp. said Tuesday it was making high-speed Internet connections through cable modems available in three more of its major markets this week.

The company launched the service Tuesday in portions of its subscriber areas in the Philadelphia area and in Orange County, Calif., and will begin offering the service to parts of suburban Detroit on Thursday.
That will make the service available in at least parts of six of Comcast's top 10 markets, company officials said.

The service, called Comcast(at)Home (Editors: (at) stands for the "at" sign on the computer keyboard), allows computer users to connect to the Internet through a high-speed modem attached to Comcast's coaxial television cable. It connects users to World Wide Web content organised according to local and national interests.
The service currently operates at about 1 million to 2 million characters per second, compared with about 33,000 characters per second through common modems using dial-up telephone lines.
That enables much quicker downloading of images, video clips and other information than ordinary home dial-up systems, whose frequent slowness has earned the Web the nickname "World Wide Wait."

Jim Maguire, general manager of Comcast's Comcast Online division, said in an interview that the system is technically capable of handling transmission speeds of 10 million characters per second, although that exceeds the capacity of many personal computers.
The system uses a proprietary "pipeline" developed by privately held (at)Home Network to deliver data at high speeds to regional centres near local service areas.
It also employs local network computers to build storehouses of popular Internet sites and hasten user access.
Comcast is already providing the service in parts of Baltimore, northern New Jersey and Sarasota, Fla.

(at)Home Network is owned jointly by Comcast, Cox Communications Inc. and investor group Kleiner Perkins Caufield & Byers -- with a 14 percent interest each -- and cable giant Tele-Communications Inc., which owns 45 percent. The cable TV service providers together reach about 40 percent of U.S. homes.
Microsoft Corp. on June 9 announced a $1 billion investment in Comcast aimed at hastening the convergence of computers and cable television.
